summary: For bounded gonality and sufficiently large prime level, every curve on the diagonal modular quotient lies on a cyclic Hecke locus. The roadmap combines compact hyperbolic geometry, arithmetic repulsion and ramification estimates, and then proves the linear-torsion descent bridge for nonisotrivial elliptic families over every algebraically closed characteristic-zero field.

nodes.title: Projective p-frames: conventions on the imported projective level curve
nodes.statement: This roadmap's X(p) is the projective level curve of ModularCurvesPartII:R13.4a/projective-scalar-coarse-quotient, taken over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field: for a prime p>3, the coarse quotient of honest full level p by scalar change of frame, compactified by p-gons, with two geometric components labelled by the Weil-pairing value of a frame modulo squares and [−1] still an automorphism of every point. This node fixes the conventions used here: G=PGL₂(F_p) acts on the left by g·(E,[φ])=(E,[φ∘g̃⁻¹]) for any lift g̃, its component stabilizer is PSL₂(F_p), and one component is selected and identified with the fixed-pairing curve, the other being its transport by an element of nonsquare determinant. It constructs no new elliptic, level or compactified object.
proofSteps: Read the two components, the effective PSL₂(F_p) action, the [−1] inertia and the p-gon compactification from the owner node; the component count is also R12.2/projective-prime-level-application.
Descend the right GL₂ action on frames to a left G-action through the inverse, and compare the selected component with the fixed-pairing Γ(p) quotient, accounting for the central ±I.

Complex conjugation sends the pairing value ζ to ζ⁻¹ (R12.6/complex-conjugation-comparison), which changes the square class by −1; characteristic-zero base change commutes with the scalar quotient by flat base change of invariants.
acceptance: For p=7 the frames (e₁,e₂) and (e₁,3e₂) lie on different components, since 3 is not a square modulo 7, while (e₁,e₂) and (2e₁,2e₂) are the same projective frame.
PGL₂(F_p) permutes the two components transitively, PSL₂(F_p) is the stabilizer of each, and the scalar −I acts trivially.
[−1] preserves every projective frame, so the curve is not a fine moduli space (finding E15).
Complex conjugation preserves each component when p≡1 mod 4 and exchanges them when p≡3 mod 4.

nodes.title: The diagonal quotient surface
nodes.statement: Let S=X(p)×X(p) and Z(p)=S/G for the diagonal projective-frame action. This is a normal projective coarse surface, finite below S. Its smooth-level geometric points classify (E₁,E₂,[ψ]) with ψ:E₁[p]≃E₂[p] up to common scalar. The square class of det ψ labels its two components. For each determinant square class choose a fixed-pairing component presentation by a diagonal, possibly conjugated, PSL₂ action; changing the auxiliary nonsquare gives an equivariantly isomorphic presentation.
proofSteps: Apply the finite quotient universal property to S, using a norm of an ample line bundle to supply an invariant projective embedding.
Composition φ₂φ₁⁻¹ is invariant under simultaneous framing change. Conversely two framed presentations of the same triple differ by a diagonal element of G.

Reduce each G-orbit to a selected first component. Its stabilizer is PSL₂, while the second component records the determinant square class; a chosen nonsquare identifies that component with the first and conjugates its action. Prove independence before using the erratum’s fixed-pairing notation.
acceptance: A generic fibre of X_ε×X_ε′→Z(p) has exactly |PSL₂(F_p)|=p(p²−1)/2 points; for p=7 this is 168.
Every diagonal point (x,x) maps to the triple (E,E,[id]), and swapping the factors sends the class of ψ to the class of ψ⁻¹.

sources.match: §2.3 defines Z(p) as the coarse space of triples (E₁,E₂,ψ) with ψ a projective isomorphism of p-torsion and identifies it with the quotient of X(p)×X(p) by the diagonal PGL₂(F_p) action through (E₁,φ₁)×(E₂,φ₂)↦(E₁,E₂,φ₂φ₁⁻¹); erratum §1 writes the same surface as a PSL₂(F_p) quotient in the fixed-pairing convention. The node records both presentations and how they compare.

nodes.title: Heegner and anti-Heegner CM strata
nodes.statement: A smooth-level pair (x,y) belongs to CM only when its two projective point stabilizers share a nonidentity element. Choose corresponding nontrivial automorphisms of E_x,E_y with matching characteristic polynomial, allowing a simultaneous sign adjustment. Put the pair in CM⁺ when their tangent eigenvalues agree and in CM⁻ when they are conjugate unequal eigenvalues. This definition is independent of the common generator, compatible lifts and projective frame representatives. Equal j-invariants alone do not define CM.
proofSteps: Use the faithful derivative character of the effective cyclic stabilizer of order 2 or 3. Changing the common generator applies the same power to both eigenvalues, preserving agreement versus opposition.
Check the order-3 lifts using t²+t+I=0, and the order-4 lift using t²=−I. These are different polynomials.

Conjugating the second complex structure interchanges CM⁺ and CM⁻; simultaneous G action preserves each. Over another characteristic-zero algebraically closed field formulate the same distinction by the algebraic tangent character, transporting through an embedding only for the metric.
acceptance: For x over j=1728 the pair (x,x) is CM⁺ and (x,x̄) is CM⁻; no pair lies in both strata.
A pair with x over j=1728 and y over j=0 is in neither stratum: the stabilizer orders 2 and 3 are coprime.

The node is that definition with the independence of the choices made explicit.

nodes.title: Singular bicusps
nodes.statement: SBC⊂S consists of pairs of cusps with a common nonidentity projective stabilizer. Each individual cusp stabilizer is cyclic of order p, so their nontrivial intersection means the same order-p subgroup. A pair of arbitrary cusps is not automatically singular. The notion is G-invariant and descends to Z.
proofSteps: Use the imported cusp charts and effective order-p inertia. Equality of order-p subgroups is a group fact.
Compare with the p-gon boundary moduli, retaining μ_p rather than an unchosen constant-group identification before passing to an algebraically closed field.
Check independence of scalars and components in the full G action; conjugation and characteristic-zero base change transport the boundary and inertia.
acceptance: On one component a fixed cusp c forms a singular bicusp with exactly (p−1)/2 cusps of that component, namely those whose label spans the same line of F_p² as c's, c itself included; for p=7 there are 3.
A cusp paired with any point of Y(p) is never singular, since no nonidentity element fixes both.

nodes.title: Exhaustive quotient branch locus
nodes.statement: For p>3, the nonfree locus of S→Z(p) is exactly CM⁺∪CM⁻∪SBC. The effective stabilizer of a point of this locus is cyclic: of order 2 at CM points (of either sign) over j=1728, of order 3 at CM points over j=0, and of order p at singular bicusps. There is no mixed elliptic/cusp branch stratum.
proofSteps: A nonidentity element fixing a pair fixes both coordinates. On X(p) its stabilizers occur only over j=1728, j=0 and the cusp, with orders 2,3,p.
Since these orders are pairwise coprime, a common element forces the same type. Split the two CM tangent characters, or identify the cusp subgroups.
acceptance: Test all nine pairs of coordinate inertia types, including ordinary points with trivial inertia.

sources.match: §2.1 lists the ramification of X(p)→X(1): the cusps with index p and the points over j=1728 and j=0 with indices 2 and 3. §2.4 observes that (x,y) ramifies in X(p)×X(p)→Z(p) exactly when x and y share a nonidentity stabilizer, so both are cusps or both lie in Y(p), and names the CM⁺, CM⁻ and SBC loci. The node combines the two into the exhaustive list with stabilizer orders.

nodes.title: Cyclic Hecke loci and weighted pull-push
nodes.statement: For m≥1 with p∤m let T_m⊂S be the cyclic degree-m correspondence of ModularCurvesPartII:R14.1/projective-boundary-hecke-and-degree on the projective level curve, [φ₂]=[f[p]φ₁] for a cyclic isogeny f of degree m, with its p-gon boundary maps. Let H_m be its finite image in Z(p); a Hecke curve is an irreducible component of H_m. The weighted pull-push T_m*C=(id×a)_*(id×b)^*C of an effective one-cycle satisfies Deg(T_m*C)=ψ(m)Deg(C) with ψ(m)=m∏_{ℓ|m}(1+1/ℓ)≪m², as the owner node states. This node adds only H_m, the Hecke curves and the restrictions to S used here.
proofSteps: Take T_m, its projections, boundary extension and degree identity from R14.1/projective-boundary-hecke-and-degree, which uses the cyclic count ψ(m) and records σ₁(m) only for the full-subgroup convention.
Define H_m as the image of T_m under the finite map S→Z(p) and check its independence of the scalar representatives and its determinant component, which is multiplied by the class of m.
Apply flat pullback and proper pushforward with the projection formula for weighted cycles; transport under conjugation and characteristic-zero base change through R12.6.
acceptance: ψ(m) is the number of cyclic subgroups of order m in (Z/mZ)²: ψ(4)=6, ψ(6)=12 and ψ(9)=12, checked by direct enumeration.
T_m is invariant under the diagonal PGL₂(F_p) action and under swapping the factors, because the dual of a cyclic isogeny of degree m is cyclic of degree m.

sources.match: §2.5 defines T_n⊂X(p)×X(p) as the closure of framed pairs related by a cyclic isogeny of degree n, extends it to p-gons by explicit maps of polygons, notes its diagonal PGL₂ invariance, gives each projection degree as σ₁(n), and defines the pull-push T_m^*=μ_*ν^*. The node uses the cyclic count ψ(m) instead of σ₁(m) (finding E6) and records the degree identity for the pull-push.

nodes.title: Compact triangle uniformization
nodes.statement: For prime p>5, the orbifold with underlying X(1) and cone orders (2,3,p) is uniformized by the orientation-preserving hyperbolic triangle group Δ(2,3,p). The quotient γ_p:PSL₂(Z)→Δ sends the standard cusp translation U to an order-p rotation. For Ξ(p)=γ_p(Γ(p)), the torsion-free compact quotient Ξ(p)\H is a selected component X(p). Its deck group is PSL₂(F_p); obtain the other component by the projective-frame transport. The cusped quotient Γ(p)\H and compact quotient Ξ(p)\H have distinct universal covers/maps.
proofSteps: Use Fuchsian polygon and orbifold-covering theory for angles π/2,π/3,π/p, whose sum is <π exactly when p>6.
Identify the compactification map on orbifold fundamental groups: kill the pth power of a peripheral generator. Its normal closure is contained in Γ(p), yielding the finite deck quotient.
Use R12.3/R13.4b for the algebraic compactification and ComplexComparisonPartII for comparison; prove torsion-freeness of Ξ from the actual level cover and its local ramification.
acceptance: p=7 is hyperbolic; p=2,3,5 has spherical signature and cannot enter this metric argument.

The node states this uniformization.

nodes.title: Triangle coordinates and deformation matrices
nodes.statement: Normalize the order-2, p and 3 vertices to i, i y_p and e^{iθ_p}. Then y_p=p/π+O(p⁻¹), θ_p=π/3+O(p⁻¹). Equivalently choose θ=π/p, c=cos θ, b=(1+√(1−4sin²θ))/2 and U_p=[[c,b],[b−1,c]], S=[[0,−1],[1,0]], L_p=S U_p⁻¹ S⁻¹. Their projective classes satisfy S²=U_p^p=(S U_p)³=1 and give the normalized faithful triangle representation; U_p→[[1,1],[0,1]], L_p→[[1,0],[1,1]]. Here y_p=√(b/(1−b)).
proofSteps: Use the hyperbolic cosine rule for the triangle, or compute fixed points of these matrices. det U_p=c²−b(b−1)=1 and tr(SU_p)=1 verify the three orders.
Choose the branch b>1/2 for p>6, so the cusp vertex lies above i. Compare with the canonical triangle by the uniqueness of its angles and marked orientation.
Taylor expansion gives 1−b=π²/p²+O(p⁻⁴); derive y_p and the third vertex. Conjugate the normalization for another component rather than choosing a second metric.
acceptance: At p=7, y_p=√(b/(1−b))≈1.7251 agrees with the root of y+1/y=1/sin(π/7) given by the cosine law; at p=101, (1−b)p²/π²≈1.0006.
S²=U_p^p=(SU_p)³=−I hold for the displayed real matrices (checked numerically at p=7).

The matrices U_p and L_p are this roadmap's explicit normalization of the same triangle representation; the source does not write them.

nodes.title: A systolic witness surviving cusp filling
nodes.statement: For sufficiently large prime p write p=3r+x with x∈{1,2}. The integral matrix M_p=[[1+xp,3p],[p(2−x²+2px)/3,1+2p²−xp]] belongs to Γ(p), has trace 2p²+2, and its image under the compact triangle representation has absolute trace (27/(4π²))p²+O(p). Thus its image in Ξ(p) is hyperbolic and nonidentity. Its cusped and compact geodesic lengths are both 4 log p+O(1), giving the required upper bounds for geodesics nontrivial after cusp filling.
proofSteps: Verify integrality, determinant one and reduction to I. With U(t)=[[1,t],[0,1]] and L(t)=[[1,0],[t,1]], factor M_p=−L(2r)U(3)L(−r−1)U(3) if x=1; if x=2 use L(2r+1)U(−3)L(−r−1)U(1)L(1)U(1). These are exact integer identities.

Substitute U_p,L_p into each word. The two large lower powers divided by p converge to ±(√3/(2π))N with N=[[0,0],[1,0]], and have bounded remainder. The fixed-power words converge to U(±3), or U(1)L(1)U(1). The leading traces in both cases are 27/(4π²).
The triangle length formula 2 arcosh(|tr|/2) proves nontriviality in the compact group and the length asymptotics. This replaces the published witness U(p)L(−p), which is killed by cusp filling.
acceptance: Check the two exact word identities and the positive leading trace separately for p≡1 and p≡2 mod 3.
Check p=7 and 11 as integer examples; asymptotics alone do not specify an explicit numerical final threshold.

sources.match: Lemma 5 proves the congruence tr γ≡2 mod p² for γ∈Γ(p) and attains the minimal trace p²−2 with [[1−p²,p],[−p,1]]=U(p)L(−p), which dies when the cusps are filled (finding E12). The node replaces that witness by M_p; its two factorizations and the compact trace limit 27/(4π²) are this roadmap's computation, checked exactly and numerically for primes up to 100003.

nodes.title: Cusped systole with the filling condition
nodes.statement: Let ρ_Y be half the infimum of cusped lengths of closed geodesics whose loops remain nontrivial in X(p). Then ρ_Y=2 log p+O(1). The ordinary nonperipheral cusped systole also has length 4 log p+O(1). The factor one-half is part of the radius convention.
proofSteps: If M=I+pA has determinant one then tr M=2−p²det A, hence tr M≡2 mod p². Every hyperbolic M∈Γ(p) has |tr M|≥p²−2 and length at least 4 log p−O(1).
Use the preceding surviving witness for the matching upper bound in the smaller class of loops remaining nontrivial after filling.
acceptance: Every γ∈Γ(p) has tr γ≡2 mod p²; the values 2−p² (for U(p)L(−p)) and 2+2p² (for M_p) both occur.
At p=7 the minimal hyperbolic |trace| in Γ(7) is 47, of translation length 2arcosh(47/2)≈7.70, against 4 log 7≈7.78.

sources.match: §3.1 defines the cusped injectivity radius through geodesics that stay nontrivial in the compactification, without the factor one half of the compact definition (finding E8), and Lemma 5 states ρ_Y(p)=2 log p+O(1), proved from tr γ≡2 mod p² and the translation-length formula. The node keeps the lower-bound proof and the half-length convention.

nodes.title: Embedded cusp balls and cusp separation
nodes.statement: In the compact metric, distinct cusps have distance at least 2 log p−C. A ball of radius log p−C around a cusp is an embedded hyperbolic disc built from its incident triangle tiles. C is independent of p and the selected component.
proofSteps: Use the triangle coordinates to bound the distance from the p-vertex to its opposite side by log p−O(1). The incident p triangles give the full local disc in X(p).
Disjoint interiors of the cusp-star tiles imply separation. Transport between components with the G-action. This estimate precedes the global injectivity-radius lower bound.
acceptance: d(i,iy_p)=log y_p=log(p/π)+o(1), so the cusp star has radius log p−O(1); the two cusps iy_p and i/y_p exchanged by the order-2 rotation about i are 2 log y_p apart.

sources.locator: Lemma 6, p. 720 (tiling set up on p. 719)
sources.match: Lemma 6 states that the disc of radius log p−O(1) about a cusp meets only tiles having that cusp as a vertex, so distinct cusps are more than 2 log p−O(1) apart; the tiling of X(p) by images of the (2,3,p) triangle is set up on p. 719. The node is Lemma 6.

nodes.title: Compact and cusped metric comparison
nodes.statement: On Y(p), with r(x)=distance in h_X to the nearest cusp, tanh²(r(x)/2) h_Y(x)≤h_X(x)≤h_Y(x). On the part r≥R the length distortion is at most coth(R/2)=1+O(e^{−R}), and the pulled-back area distortion obeys the squared bound.
proofSteps: Holomorphic inclusion Y→X decreases the Kobayashi metric, giving the upper inequality h_X≤h_Y.
Lift the maximal cusp-free compact disc around x, compare the disc’s complete metric at its centre, and apply Schwarz–Pick. Separate quadratic-form comparison from length comparison.
acceptance: Near a cusp the lower comparison degenerates; no uniform compact isometry is asserted for Hecke maps.

sources.match: Proposition 7 proves tanh²(d_cusp/2)h_Y≤h_X≤h_Y on Y(p): the upper bound from the Kobayashi contraction of the inclusion Y(p)→X(p), the lower bound by comparing with the Kobayashi metric of a cusp-free disc about the point. The node is Proposition 7 with the length-distortion consequence.

nodes.title: Compact injectivity radius with repeated cusp visits
nodes.statement: For each component of X(p), ρ_X=2 log p+O(1), where ρ_X is half the shortest noncontractible closed-geodesic length. In particular the shortest length is 4 log p+O(1), rather than 2 log p+O(1).
proofSteps: The surviving witness gives the upper bound. For a shortest compact geodesic γ of length L≤4 log p+C, use disjoint embedded cusp discs of radii R_b=(1/2)log p and inner radii R_s=(1/4)log p. Every connected visit to an outer disc reaching its inner disc costs at least 2(R_b−R_s), so there are O(1) deep visits, counting repeated visits to the same cusp.

Outside the inner discs, the metric comparison costs O(e^{−R_s}L)=o(1). For each deep arc lift to its embedded hyperbolic disc, use cosh r(s)=cosh r_min cosh(s−s₀), and integrate coth(r(s)/2)−1 on r≥1 to obtain a uniform O(1) error. Replace any r<1 part by a unit-circle arc; its cusped length is O(1) by the metric comparison.

The resulting loop in Y is homotopic to γ in X and has cusped length ≤L+O(1). It is neither contractible nor peripheral in Y because its filled class is nontrivial. Apply the cusped lower bound. The argument counts visits and does not use the source’s unsupported at-most-one-cusp assertion.
acceptance: Preserve L=2ρ_X throughout.
A shortest geodesic making two deep visits is handled by two bounded errors, not ruled out by assertion.

sources.match: Corollary 8 states ρ_X(p)=2 log p+O(1): the upper bound from Lemma 5 and h_X≤h_Y, the lower bound by replacing the deep part of a shortest loop near one cusp with a boundary arc and integrating 1/tanh²(x/2)−1. The node keeps the statement; its visit-counting proof replaces the one-cusp step (finding E13).

nodes.title: Cusp coordinates and Hecke enlargement
nodes.statement: For a width-p cusp use q=exp(2πiz/p). The horoball Im z>y, y>1/p, gives an embedded disc D_y of Euclidean radius exp(−2πy/p), contained in B_X(c,2 artanh(exp(−2πy/p))). For log p+C<R<2 log p−C one has B_X(c,R)⊂D_{O(pe^{−R})}. For p∤m and log p+C<R with R+log m<2 log p−C, the inverse cyclic Hecke image of B_X(c,R) lies in the union of balls B_X(c_i,R+log m+C) at the corresponding cusps.
proofSteps: Compare the punctured q-disc and its filling by Schwarz–Pick and the compact metric inequality; use the hyperbolic radial distance to invert the radius estimate.
At a prime-to-p isogeny branch the imaginary part changes by a factor between m⁻¹ and m. Apply the q-coordinate estimate at every inverse cusp, including the boundary component map.
acceptance: Check the direction of both disc inclusions and the additive log m enlargement; do not apply outside its specified range.

sources.match: Page 721 shows that for y>1/p the horoball Im z>y embeds as a disc D_y of Euclidean radius e^{−2πy/p} about each cusp with D_y⊂B_X(c,2 artanh e^{−2πy/p}) (display (2)), that B_X(c,R)⊂D_{O(pe^{−R})} for log p+O(1)<R<2 log p−O(1) (display (3)), and in Lemma 9 that the Hecke image of a cusp ball lies in the union of balls of radius R+log m+O(1) about the image cusps. The node restates (2), (3) and Lemma 9.

nodes.title: Integral height uses the existing entrywise norm
nodes.statement: For an integral or real 2×2 matrix the paper’s height is max_{i,j}|M_ij|, exactly Mathlib’s entrywise supremum norm after the standard scalar embedding. It is not the operator or Frobenius norm. Use this existing norm with h(MN)≤2h(M)h(N), h(M⁻¹)=h(M) in SL₂, and entrywise bounds for integral minors.
proofSteps: Read Matrix.norm_eq_sup_sup_nnnorm at the pin, fix its local entrywise instance, and specialize to Fin 2.
Use the two-term multiplication formula and the adjugate inverse. These comparisons provide the arithmetic convention; no competing general matrix-height theory is defined.
acceptance: The all-ones 2×2 matrix has entrywise height 1, not Frobenius norm 2.

sources.match: §3.3 defines the height h(M) of M∈SL₂(Z) as the largest absolute value of an entry. The node identifies this with Mathlib's entrywise sup norm and records the elementary product and inverse bounds used later.

nodes.title: Short elliptic displacement has a small integral lift
nodes.statement: Fix the image ι of i, or the image ϖ of the order-3 triangle vertex, in one component. For fixed 0<δ<1/2 and large p, a component-preserving g with d(ι,gι)<δρ_X (respectively d(ϖ,gϖ)<δρ_X) has a representative γ_p(M) modulo Ξ with M∈SL₂(Z) and h(M)≤C_δp^{4δ}. No nonsquare component-switching element is represented by an SL₂(Z) reduction on this component.
proofSteps: Compare the triangle chart to the cusped chart over the relevant small ball and use the compact-radius estimate.
For M=[[a,b],[c,d]], Im(Mi)=1/(c²+d²) and Re(Mi)=(ac+bd)/(c²+d²); the hyperbolic distance formula and ad−bc=1 bound all four entries by O(e^{2R}). Take R=δρ_X. Repeat in the fixed order-3 chart.
acceptance: For M=[[a,b],[c,d]]∈SL₂(Z), cosh d_H(i,Mi)=(a²+b²+c²+d²)/2, so h(M)≤(2cosh R)^{1/2}, well within the O(e^{2R}) bound used; for M=[[2,1],[1,1]] the displacement is arcosh(7/2).
The bound concerns component-preserving deck elements only; a component-switching element of PGL₂(F_p) is not γ_p(M) for any M∈SL₂(Z).

sources.locator: Lemma 10 and the remark after it, p. 722
sources.match: Lemma 10 states that if d(ι,γι)<δρ_X(p) with δ<1/2, then γ=γ_p(M) modulo Ξ(p) with h(M)=O(p^{4δ}); its proof bounds the entries of M with d_H(i,Mi)=R by O(e^{2R}) using Im(Mi)=1/(c²+d²), the distance formula and ad−bc=1. The remark after it gives the same for the order-3 point ϖ. The node is Lemma 10 with that remark.

nodes.title: A nearby lifted cusp has a small-height description
nodes.statement: Fix the lift i y_p of a cusp c₀ and its order-p triangle stabilizer H. For fixed 0<δ<1/2 and large p, any lift z of a cusp c with d(i y_p,z)≤(1+δ)ρ_X can be written z=σ γ_p(M)i y_p for σ∈H and M∈SL₂(Z), h(M)=O_δ(p^{4δ}).
proofSteps: Cusp separation puts the lens between the two large cusp discs near the relevant triangle-star edges.
Choose an adjacent order-2 vertex, move it by σ, and apply the elliptic small-height lift. The marked adjacent cusp is recovered by the triangle combinatorics.
acceptance: The representation z=σγ_p(M)·iy_p is not unique: M may be replaced by MU^k for any integer k, since γ_p(U) fixes iy_p; the statement asserts that some representative has small height.

sources.match: Lemma 11(a) states that a lift z of a cusp with d(iy_p,z)≤(1+δ)ρ_X(p) has the form σγ_p(M)·iy_p with σ in the cusp stabilizer and h(M)=O(p^{4δ}); the proof places the overlap of the two cusp discs near an order-2 vertex and applies Lemma 10. The node is Lemma 11(a).

nodes.title: Cusp displacement controls a stabilizer double coset
nodes.statement: Under the same hypotheses, if d(c₀,gc₀)≤(1+δ)ρ_X for a component-preserving deck element g, then modulo Ξ, g∈H γ_p(M) H for some integral SL₂ matrix of height O_δ(p^{4δ}). The two H factors cannot be omitted.
proofSteps: Lift a shortest path from c₀ to gc₀ beginning at i y_p. Apply the lifted-cusp theorem to its endpoint.
The ambiguity in each marked lift is exactly its cusp stabilizer, producing the left and right H factors.
acceptance: Both stabilizer factors are needed: for nontrivial σ,σ′∈H, the element σγ_p(M)σ′ need not lie in γ_p(M)H or in Hγ_p(M).
For γ∈H itself, d(c₀,γc₀)=0 and M=I works.

sources.match: Lemma 11(b) deduces from part (a) that d(c₀,γc₀)≤(1+δ)ρ_X(p) gives γ∈H·γ_p(M)·H modulo Ξ(p) with h(M)=O(p^{4δ}), by choosing the lift realizing the distance. The node is Lemma 11(b).

nodes.title: Unique close lift of a different cusp
nodes.statement: There is δ₀>0 such that for 0<δ<δ₀ and sufficiently large p, fixed distinct cusps c₀,c in one component and a fixed lift z₀ of c₀ admit at most one lift z of c with d(z₀,z)≤(1+δ)ρ_X.
proofSteps: Apply the cusp-height theorem to two candidate lifts. Their relative matrix reduces to the upper triangular cusp normalizer.
Its relevant lower entry is O(p^{8δ}); take δ<1/8, with margin, so divisibility by p forces actual vanishing. The integral upper triangular SL₂ element maps into the cusp rotation subgroup.

The compact covering group has trivial intersection with this finite stabilizer, so the two lifts coincide. The smallness condition is strengthened from the printed numerical range rather than inferred from 8δ<2.
acceptance: The integral upper triangular elements of SL₂(Z) are ±[[1,t],[0,1]], and γ_p maps them into the cusp stabilizer; this is why two close lifts coincide.
For δ=1/10 the relative matrix has entries O(p^{0.8}), so an entry divisible by p vanishes for large p; for δ=1/5 the bound O(p^{1.6}) does not force this (finding E14).

sources.match: Proposition 12(a) states that a cusp c≠c₀ has at most one lift within (1+δ)ρ_X(p) of a fixed lift of c₀; the proof shows that the relative matrix of two such lifts is upper triangular modulo p with entries O(p^{8δ}), hence upper triangular, hence in the cusp stabilizer. The node is Proposition 12(a) with the smallness condition on δ corrected (finding E14).

nodes.title: Intersections of cusp balls lie in a small ball
nodes.statement: For sufficiently small fixed δ>0 and large p, distinct cusps c₀,c satisfy B(c₀,(1/2+δ)ρ_X)∩B(c,(1/2+δ)ρ_X)⊂B(u,δρ_X+C) for a suitable u. The constant is uniform in the cusps.
proofSteps: Lift the lens through the unique-lift result, taking its δ parameter twice as large when necessary and fixing that before p grows.
Use d(c₀,c)≥ρ_X−O(1) and the imported hyperbolic midpoint-lens bound of radius R+O(1) for two radius D+R balls with centres separated by 2D.
acceptance: In the disc model with centres ±r and s=tanh(R/2), each ball B(±r,D+R) lies in a Euclidean disc meeting the other inside the Euclidean disc of radius √s about 0, i.e. inside the hyperbolic ball of radius 2 artanh√s=R+O(1).

sources.locator: Proposition 12(b), p. 723; Lemma 13 and its proof, pp. 724–725
sources.match: Proposition 12(b) states that the (1/2+δ)ρ_X(p)-balls about two distinct cusps meet inside a ball of radius δρ_X(p)+O(1); the proof combines part (a) with Lemma 13, which places the lens of two hyperbolic balls of radius D+R whose centres are 2D apart inside a ball of radius R+O(1) about the midpoint. The node is Proposition 12(b).

nodes.title: A cusp-ball overlap count
nodes.statement: For sufficiently small fixed δ>0 and large p, every x∈X(p) lies within (1/2+δ)ρ_X of at most C_δp^{24δ} cusps in its component.
proofSteps: If there is more than one such cusp, the lens theorem puts x near an adjacent order-2 vertex. Enlarge δ by a fixed factor, fixed before p grows.
The short-displacement height bound counts the possible neighboring integral matrices by their entries, giving the stated coarse exponent. If there is at most one cusp, the bound is immediate.
acceptance: A cusp itself is within (1/2+δ)ρ_X of exactly one cusp for small δ, since distinct cusps are at least 2 log p−O(1) apart, and a point farther than (1/2+δ)ρ_X from every cusp has count zero.

sources.match: Proposition 12(c) bounds by O(p^{24δ}) the number of cusps within (1/2+δ)ρ_X(p) of a point; the proof reduces to a point near an order-2 vertex and counts the small-height matrices of Lemma 10. The node is Proposition 12(c).

nodes.title: Small equations reconstruct a signed Hecke locus
nodes.statement: Fix A. A unique invertible projective 2×2 solution over F_p of integral linear equations with coefficients bounded by p^(Aδ) has a primitive integral representative Q of height p^(O_A(δ)), for sufficiently small δ and large p. Put m=|det Q|; then p∤m. If det Q>0 its Smith form gives a cyclic degree-m holomorphic isogeny; if det Q<0, composition with the fixed real reflection gives the corresponding conjugate Hecke locus after complex realization. On cusp data the two cases give the respective ordinary or conjugate Hecke boundary incidence. Uniqueness does not determine the sign, and multiplication by −1 cannot change it.
proofSteps: Uniqueness of an invertible projective solution forces a one-dimensional kernel for p>3: in a projective line of matrices the determinant is a quadratic, so an invertible point would give at least p−1 invertible projective points. Thus the modular rank is three. A nonzero rank-three minor and its cofactors give the kernel vector. All relevant rank-four minors are bounded by p^(O_A(δ))<p, so their vanishing modulo p implies vanishing over Z; the same rational kernel is one-dimensional. The cofactor vector is nonzero modulo p and has the required height.

Divide out the gcd; reduction is still the same invertible projective matrix, so p∤det Q. Keep the sign. Positive determinant is automatic only in the definite CM centralizer application. For negative determinant factor Q as a positive-determinant matrix times the integral reflection diag(1,−1).

Use Smith normal form for the primitive positive lattice map. For a negative map use the conjugate complex structure and R12.6, then the same positive Smith form. Check the p-gon toric and component factors separately at the boundary; the sign is the ordinary versus conjugate Hecke distinction.
acceptance: A negative determinant lift gives an antiholomorphic correspondence and is not silently called a Hecke isogeny.

sources.locator: Proofs of Lemma 15 (pp. 726–727), Proposition 17 case (2) (p. 728) and Proposition 18 case 2(2) (p. 731)
sources.match: Each of these proofs reconstructs the unique projective solution of small integral linear equations as an integral matrix of height p^{O(δ)} and reads a Hecke index off its determinant. The node isolates that reconstruction; keeping the sign of the determinant is this roadmap's correction (findings E18, E19).

nodes.title: The distinct-Heegner centralizer equations have rank three
nodes.statement: In the nearby distinct-Heegner setup let t₀=[[0,1],[-1,0]] or [[0,1],[-1,-1]], and let M_x,M_y be the short integral lifts. The simultaneous equations t₀g=gt₀ and t₀M_y⁻¹gM_x=M_y⁻¹gM_x t₀ have solution space of dimension at most one over F_p for sufficiently small δ. For the second t₀ use t₀²+t₀+I=0 and det(aI+bt₀)=a²−ab+b²; for the first use a²+b².
proofSteps: The first centralizer is the two-dimensional span of I,t₀. If the second relation is redundant, M_x,M_y normalize that quadratic algebra.

Small-height congruences lift the trace/determinant polynomial to Q. The positive-determinant rational normalizer of the imaginary quadratic algebra is its centralizer; the conjugating coset has negative determinant.
Integral determinant-one centralizer elements are the finite Gaussian or Eisenstein units, hence stabilize the corresponding elliptic vertex. This contradicts distinctness of the two Heegner points.
acceptance: For t₀=[[0,1],[−1,0]] the centralizer is {aI+bt₀} with determinant a²+b², whose determinant-one integral elements are the four units ±I, ±t₀; for t₀=[[0,1],[−1,−1]] the determinant is a²−ab+b² and there are six units ±I, ±t₀, ±t₀².

The rational normalizer of the centralizer contains elements of negative determinant, such as diag(1,−1) for the order-4 case; only positive-determinant normalizing elements are forced into the centralizer.

sources.match: Lemma 15 states that for large p the solutions g∈M₂(F_p) of [t,g]=1 and [t,M_y⁻¹gM_x]=1 form a space of dimension at most one; the proof shows that otherwise M_x and M_y normalize the centralizer of t₀, hence lie in it, contradicting distinctness of the CM points. The node is Lemma 15 with the order-3 relation corrected (finding E5).

nodes.title: Heegner-only repulsion
nodes.statement: There are absolute δ₀,A>0 such that for fixed 0<δ<δ₀ and sufficiently large p, two distinct points of CM⁺ with the same image in X(1)² and intersecting radius-δρ_X max-product balls both lie on one T_m with m≤C_δp^{Aδ}, p∤m. There is no corresponding conclusion with T_m for CM⁻.
proofSteps: Move the first pair to a marked elliptic vertex and its commuting projective element. For CM⁺ the normalizer representative is h₀=1; no integral lift of the nonidentity normalizer coset is used.
Lift both short displacements, apply the centralizer rank bound, and reconstruct a small positive determinant representative in the definite quadratic algebra.
Apply cyclic-isogeny reconstruction to both framed pairs. Transport the statement under the full component action.
acceptance: Two distinct Heegner points over the same pair of CM points that both lie on the diagonal T₁ satisfy the conclusion with m=1.
The conclusion fails for CM⁻: conjugating the second factor carries a close CM⁺ pair on T_m to a close CM⁻ pair on T̄_m, which meets no ordinary Hecke locus.

sources.match: Erratum Proposition 2.1 restates published Proposition 14 for Heegner points only: two distinct CM⁺ points with the same image in X(1)×X(1) and intersecting δρ_X(p)-balls lie on a Hecke divisor T_m with m=p^{O(δ)}. The erratum says the published proof works with h₀=1 and that in general no integral lift of the other normalizer coset exists. The node is that statement.

nodes.title: Conjugate Hecke loci are real analytic
nodes.statement: In the same smooth real product, let c₂ be complex conjugation on the second factor and put T̄_m=c₂(T_m). This is a real analytic, generally totally real locus for the original product complex structure, not an algebraic or complex analytic divisor. Conjugation transports CM⁺ to CM⁻ and Heegner repulsion to these loci. No intersection number C·T̄_m is defined here.
proofSteps: Take the set image under the antiholomorphic isometry in one factor. Keep the conjugate complex structure explicit when applying the imported conjugate-diagonal volume estimate.
Define neighborhoods by the transported max metric; retain complex curves and their original complex orientation for area integration.
Use R12.6 to make the component and conjugation comparisons. The underlying algebraic Hecke correspondences base change, while this real analytic construction is made only after complex realization.
acceptance: T̄₁ is the graph of complex conjugation on X(p); its tangent planes contain no complex line, and it meets the complex curve T₁ along the points fixed by conjugation.

sources.match: Erratum §1 explains that conjugating the second factor preserves the metric and exchanges Heegner and anti-Heegner points, so that nearby anti-Heegner points lie on low-degree conjugate Hecke curves; §4.1 writes these loci as T̄_m and remarks that the multiplicity of a curve along T̄_m has no meaning. The node defines T̄_m and records these properties.

nodes.title: Hecke curves avoid anti-Heegner CM points
nodes.statement: For p∤m one has T_m∩CM⁻=∅. The genuine cyclic isogeny intertwines the compatible automorphism on tangent spaces, so the CM signs agree. This does not imply that distinct anti-Heegner points repel in the ordinary Hecke sense.
proofSteps: An ordinary Hecke point in CM must have both elliptic curves of the same CM type: different imaginary-quadratic endomorphism algebras cannot be isogenous. Over C identify the two j=1728 curves, or the two j=0 curves, by an isomorphism. The isogeny becomes an element of the commutative CM endomorphism ring, hence intertwines the automorphisms with equal tangent eigenvalue. The opposite automorphism cannot induce the same torsion intertwining when p>3 and the isogeny is prime to p.
A nonzero complex-linear derivative preserves the chosen CM tangent eigenvalue, excluding the opposite character.
acceptance: Do not reuse the false deduction that all CM⁻ points therefore have disjoint large balls.

sources.match: Remark 16 asserts that Hecke curves do not pass through anti-Heegner CM points and deduces that anti-Heegner points repel; erratum §1 keeps the first assertion and withdraws the deduction. The node is the first assertion, proved through the commuting CM endomorphisms.

nodes.title: Three-bicusp repulsion with both determinant signs
nodes.statement: There are δ₀,A>0 such that for fixed 0<δ<δ₀ and large p, if a point of S is within (1/2+δ)ρ_X of at least three distinct singular bicusps, every SBC point in that ball lies on one ordinary or conjugate Hecke locus of index m≤C_δp^(Aδ), p∤m. Two bicusps do not force the reconstruction. The positive-Hecke-only formulation is not used: its proof has an uncontrolled determinant sign, and the reader gives a negative-reflection cusp example. Moreover the original point is within Aδρ_X+C_δ of that signed locus and each of its coordinates has distance at least (1/2−Aδ)ρ_X−C_δ from every cusp. These strengthened outputs use the same height reconstruction, not a new repulsion premise.
proofSteps: Use cusp double cosets and unique lifts to encode each nearby bicusp as a prescribed image of a point of P¹(F_p). If only at most two distinct source points are specified, the small integral upper-triangular lift argument leaves at most two bicusps.

Three distinct prescribed projective-line images determine Q up to scalar. Cofactors give the small primitive integral representative, retaining both determinant signs. Its invertible reduction makes p∤|det Q|.

For positive determinant use the ordinary cyclic isogeny boundary; for negative determinant compose with the fixed reflection and use the conjugate boundary. The same reconstructed Q satisfies every nearby bicusp condition, so all lie on the same signed locus. No unproved orientation assumption is inserted.

With at least three bicusps, the cusp-normalizer argument forces at least two distinct cusp coordinates in each factor. Separation then bounds the distance from every cusp below by (1/2−O(δ))ρ_X. The two-cusp lens puts each factor within O(δρ_X) of an order-two vertex. Move those vertices to (ι,gι); the same small signed matrix representing g gives a point of the signed Hecke correspondence within O(log h(Q))=O(δρ_X), using h_X≤h_Y and the positive Smith form or its reflected version. This places the original point in the thin signed tube on the cusp complement.
acceptance: Check sharp distinction between two prescribed images (a one-parameter projective freedom) and three (uniqueness).
For p≡1 mod4 and a²=−1, the nearby cusp pairs (v,av) have negative-reflection type; they do not lie on T_m with m<p−1.

sources.match: Proposition 17 states that if a point is within (1/2+δ)ρ_X(p) of at least three singular bicusps, all singular bicusps that close to it lie on one Hecke divisor T_m with m=p^{O(δ)}; the proof encodes each bicusp as a prescribed image of a point of P¹(F_p) and reconstructs g from three of them. The node keeps the proof, allows a negative determinant (finding E18), and adds the two metric consequences used in GF.5.

nodes.title: Big diagonals and small Hecke curves
nodes.statement: For g∈G define Δ_g={(gx,gy,x,y):(x,y)∈S}⊂S². For p∤m define τ_{g,m}=Δ_g restricted to (x,y)∈T_m. In the max-product distance, B(Δ_g,R) is exactly the locus d(x₁,gx₂)<2R and d(y₁,gy₂)<2R. Here Δ_g has complex codimension two in S²; multiplicity along it means the sum of local curve-point multiplicities at its finite intersection, not a Cartier divisor intersection. Also define the real analytic signed companion τ̄_(g,m) by restricting Δ_g to T̄_m. Only τ_(g,m) is a holomorphic small Hecke curve.
proofSteps: Use the graph of the diagonal action on both coordinates. Midpoints of the two coordinate geodesics prove the factor-two tube formula; the triangle inequality proves the converse.
Restrict the same graph to the imported T_m. Check group relabeling on both slots, inversion on slot swap, and the component restrictions explicitly.
Algebraic loci commute with characteristic-zero base change; after complex realization conjugation transports graph, Hecke index and max distance.
acceptance: For g≠h, Δ_g∩Δ_h consists of points over pairs (x,y) fixed by h⁻¹g, so distinct big diagonals meet only over the finite branch locus CM⁺∪CM⁻∪SBC.
Δ_g is a surface in the fourfold S², so a curve meets it in finitely many points unless it lies in it.

nodes.title: Quadratic centralizers give only logarithmically many small elements
nodes.statement: For a nonscalar rational 2×2 matrix N whose algebra Q[N] is reduced, the determinant-one integral elements in its centralizer with entrywise height ≤p^A have O_A(log p) possibilities, uniformly in N and its embedding. A nonreduced quadratic algebra is the unipotent case and must be returned to the cusp branch. Scalar common centralizers impose no rigidity and must be eliminated by additional intertwining equations.
proofSteps: In the imaginary quadratic case integral norm-one eigenvalues are roots of unity, leaving an absolute bound. In the split rational case they are rational algebraic integer units, hence ±1.

In the real quadratic case log of the absolute first eigenvalue embeds the norm-one unit group modulo a finite kernel into R. The trace of a nontrivial positive unit is an integer ≥3, giving a uniform positive separation for the logarithms. An eigenvalue has absolute value ≤2h(M), so only O_A(log p) separated values occur.
If the minimal polynomial has a repeated root, isolate its nilpotent part and its rational fixed line; this is the cusp/unipotent configuration, where the logarithmic count is not claimed.
acceptance: Upper unipotent matrices of height p^A have polynomially many parameters and are excluded from this logarithmic conclusion.

sources.match: In part (1) of Case 2 the span of the small elements is a torus, which is lifted to a rational torus; its small elements are then powers of one semisimple element, of which only O(log p) have height p^{O(δ)}, while the nilpotent case is returned to part (a). The node states the uniform count behind that step.

nodes.title: Diagonal-overlap dichotomy
nodes.statement: There exist absolute constants A,C,δ₀>0 such that for fixed 0<δ<δ₀, all sufficiently large p and ξ∈S², membership in more than C log p distinct tubes B(Δ_g,δρ_X) forces one of: (a) ξ is within (1/2+Aδ)ρ_X+C of a point of SBC×SBC; (b) ξ is within Aδρ_X+C of an ordinary small Hecke curve τ_{g,m} or its real analytic conjugate companion τ̄_{g,m} with m≤C_δp^{Aδ}. All constants are independent of the curve integrated through ξ.
proofSteps: Near a cusp in one coordinate, cusp separation forces all relevant deck transformations into one cusp-stabilizer coset. Cusp height and normalizer arguments put the other coordinate near a cusp with the same stabilizer, giving (a).
Away from all deep cusp neighborhoods, move to nearby marked elliptic vertices and lift each short displacement. Distinct lifts give pairs of small integral conjugacy equations.

If the common quadratic algebra is reduced and nonscalar, the uniform unit count gives O(log p). A nilpotent relation returns to the cusp branch. In the scalar-centralizer case reconstruct the unique small integral projective intertwiner from at most three relations. Its determinant is nonzero but can have either sign: use the positive lattice map for τ_(g,m), or factor the reflection and use τ̄_(g,m). The displacement bounds use h_X≤h_Y and the corresponding conjugate isometry.
acceptance: Quantify C log p as a uniform finite threshold, rather than treating ω(log p) as a predicate on a single point.

sources.match: Proposition 18 states that a point lying in ω(log p) of the tubes B(Δ_g,δρ_X(p)) is within (1/2+O(δ))ρ_X(p) of a point whose two projections are singular bicusps, or within O(δ)ρ_X(p) of a small Hecke curve τ_{g,m} with m=p^{O(δ)}; the proof splits by whether a coordinate is near a cusp and then by the centralizer of the span of the small elements. The node is that dichotomy with a C log p threshold and with the conjugate branch added (finding E19).

nodes.title: Quantitative cusp-rotation overlap
nodes.statement: In the cusp branch of the overlap proof the relevant g lie in a single order-p stabilizer coset. At distance d>0 from its fixed cusp, the number moving a coordinate less than 2R is at most C min(p,1+p sinh(R)/sinh(d)). For a fixed pair of projected bicusp centres a₁,a₂ in the cusp-branch decomposition, the transformations carrying a₂ to a₁ form one order-p stabilizer coset. The short-displacement comparison can be made in either slot separately, by taking inverses; use the farther of that slot’s two cusp coordinates, so d=d_S(z_i,a_i). With R=O(δρ_X), this gives O(1+p^{1+Aδ}e^{−d}) for d≥1 and O(p) for d<1. At d=0 use p directly. The weaker shell bound with an exponential O(δρ_X) loss is sufficient for diagonal multiplicity.
proofSteps: Attach the two projected bicusp centres from the cusp-branch lift. The deck transformation sends the source centre to the target centre. Fixing a pair leaves a coset of the source stabilizer, of order p. Two short transformations in this coset differ by a rotation with O(δρ_X) displacement. Apply this to the source slot and, by inversion, to the target slot. The radius R₀+O(δρ_X)<ρ_X ensures the short lifts agree.
For a rotation through 2πk/p in an embedded hyperbolic disc, compute sinh(distance(z,g^kz)/2)=sinh(d)|sin(πk/p)|.
Count the equally spaced angles satisfying this inequality and include the identity by the additive 1. The two coordinate inequalities only reduce the count.
For R growing like δlog p, retain sinh(R); replacing it by R is unjustified. Absorb exp(O(δρ_X)) in p^{Aδ} after all constants are fixed.
acceptance: R→0 recovers a bound proportional to pR/sinh d plus 1.
For R=δρ_X growing with p, test sinh R instead of its small-R linear approximation.

The node replaces that circumference count by the exact rotation identity (finding E16).

nodes.title: Canonical degree and weighted multiplicity adapters
nodes.statement: Use the imported effective curve cycles on X(p)^r. For a normalized map ν:D→X(p)^r, put Deg(ν_*[D])=deg_D ν* K_{X(p)^r}=Σ_j deg(pr_jν)(2g_X−2), with degree zero for a constant coordinate. Equivalently vol=2πDeg. Local multiplicities of a pushforward include the map degree over its image. Point-sums along a big diagonal and divisor intersection along a small diagonal remain different operations.
proofSteps: Apply the imported cycle normalization and weighted pushforward, then the canonical-area theorem coordinate by coordinate.
Use the projection formula to identify algebraic and analytic degrees under C2/C5. No area factor remains inside the algebraic largest-projection inequality.
acceptance: The diagonal map D=X→X² has degree 2(2g_X−2).
A q-fold cover of a curve image multiplies volume, degree and local pushforward multiplicity by q.
A constant cusp coordinate contributes zero to the degree.

nodes.title: Heegner multiplicity decay
nodes.statement: Fix δ₁>0 small and then δ₂>0 sufficiently small in terms of δ₁. For all sufficiently large p and every effective one-cycle C⊂S with no Hecke component, mult_CM⁺(C)≤C_{δ₁,δ₂}(p^{−2δ₂}+p^{3δ₁−1})Deg(C). Thus for some η>0, uniformly in C, mult_CM⁺(C)=O(p^{−η}Deg(C)).
proofSteps: Put d=p^{δ₁}. Off the union of T_m with m<d, corrected Heegner repulsion makes the δ₂ρ_X balls disjoint after splitting the two elliptic types. Point-volume bounds cost a(δ₂ρ_X)⁻¹=O(p^{−2δ₂}).

On the small Hecke union, use weighted Hecke pull-push and the ordinary diagonal volume bound, or its intersection corollary. The fixed-radius CM balls on the diagonal are disjoint, and a radius almost ρ_X/2 yields a p⁻¹ factor.
Sum ψ(m)≪m² for m<d, giving d³. Choose 3δ₁<1 and η<min(2δ₂,1−3δ₁) before choosing p.
acceptance: With d=p^{δ₁}, Σ_{m<d}ψ(m)≍d³, so the near-Hecke term p^{3δ₁−1} decays exactly when δ₁<1/3.
The order of choices matters: if δ₂ is not small relative to δ₁, two close CM⁺ points off the small Hecke union may lie on some T_m with m≥d, and the balls are no longer disjoint.

Erratum §4.1 says this proof covers only Heegner points. The node is the Heegner case with the two exponents separated.

nodes.title: Anti-Heegner multiplicity decay
nodes.statement: With independent small δ₁,δ₂ chosen as above, every effective non-Hecke one-cycle C⊂S satisfies mult_CM⁻(C)≤C_{δ₁,δ₂}(p^{−2δ₂}+p^{3δ₁−1})Deg(C) for all sufficiently large p. In particular it is O(p^{−η}Deg(C)) for a fixed η>0. This estimate does not use an intersection product with a conjugate Hecke locus.
proofSteps: Split CM⁻ into points off and on the small T̄_m union. Isometric transport of the corrected repulsion gives the disjoint-ball estimate off that union.
For points on T̄_m, apply the holomorphic Hecke pull-push to C and use fixed ε-balls at the CM⁻ points on the conjugate diagonal. Their volumes are bounded by the ε-tube volume.

The imported conjugate-diagonal ratio gives V(ε)≤(sinh ε/sinh R)V(R), taking R approaching ρ_X/2 from below. This is O(p⁻¹) times the total cycle volume. The ratio is the reciprocal of the erratum’s misprinted line. Sum the O(d³) Hecke degree costs.
acceptance: For fixed ε the volume factor sinh ε/sinh R is ≍p⁻¹ as R increases to ρ_X/2=log p+O(1); with the erratum's printed reciprocal it would grow like p.

The node is Proposition 4.1 with the displayed volume ratio inverted (finding E4).

nodes.title: The stronger singular-bicusp multiplicity bound
nodes.statement: Choose δ₃>0 small first, independently of δ₁,δ₂. Then choose δ₁>0 so small that 3δ₁<2δ₃, and δ₂>0 a sufficiently small positive multiple of δ₁ as required by bicusp repulsion. For d=p^{δ₁}, T=SBC∩⋃_{m<d}(T_m∪T̄_m) and S₀=SBC−T, every effective non-Hecke C⊂S satisfies mult_{S₀}(C)≪p^{−1−2δ₂}Deg(C) and mult_T(C)≪p^{−1−2δ₃+3δ₁}Deg(C). Consequently p mult_SBC(C)=O(p^{−η}Deg(C)) for any fixed 0<η<min(2δ₂,2δ₃−3δ₁).
proofSteps: Use signed three-bicusp repulsion, so balls centered off the ordinary-and-conjugate small-Hecke union overlap at most twice. Point-volume gives p^(−1−2δ₂).

For each signed locus pull back by the holomorphic cyclic Hecke correspondence to the ordinary or conjugate diagonal. Balls centered at its SBC points have radius (1/2+δ₃)ρ_X. If at least two overlap, the midpoint lens places the point within δ₃ρ_X+O(1) of that diagonal, using conjugation as an isometry in the negative case. The cusp count bounds the overlap by p^(24δ₃), with a fixed extra constant in δ₃ allowed.

The isolated-ball contribution is p^(−1−2δ₃) times ψ(m)Deg(C). The multiple-overlap contribution is bounded by p^(−1−2δ₃) p^(Bδ₃) p^(−1+2δ₃) ψ(m)Deg(C), using cosh for the ordinary diagonal and sinh for the conjugate diagonal. First fix δ₃ with (B+2)δ₃<1; then this is at most the isolated contribution. Sum ψ(m) for m<d to obtain p^(−1−2δ₃+3δ₁), and choose 3δ₁<2δ₃. This adds the missing negative-sign branch to the author erratum argument.
acceptance: The output is p·mult_SBC=o(Deg), which absorbs order-p inertia.
The weaker p^{−1+ε} bound does not pass this acceptance check.

The node is Proposition 4.2 with the conjugate loci added (finding E18) and the overlap multiplicity counted (finding E22).

nodes.title: Projectionwise cusped-volume measure
nodes.statement: For a normalized effective curve cycle ν:D→X(p)^r define its cusped area measure as the weighted sum of the extensions of (pr_jν)*ω_Y over each nonconstant coordinate. A constant coordinate contributes zero, including a coordinate constantly equal to a cusp. At a nonconstant cusp preimage use the integrable punctured-disc density, with no point atom. The compact area measure is defined by the analogous sum with ω_X. Their difference is a positive finite measure.
proofSteps: Use the imported cusp-pullback integration theorem. Locally q(t)=t^e u(t), e>0, gives an integrable density proportional to 1/(|t|² log²|t|); it is not evaluation of a singular two-form at a constant cusp map.
Apply the compact-versus-cusped metric comparison to nonconstant coordinates. Linearity handles effective cycles and weighted maps.

For each nonconstant projection of degree d_j the total areas are d_j times the total base-curve areas, by the finite-map integration formula; constant coordinates have d_j=0. All constructions are independent of normalization parameters.
acceptance: For the diagonal curve t↦(t,t) in X(p)² the cusped and compact measures are twice the pulled-back areas of Y(p) and X(p), with total masses in ratio Area(Y)/Area(X)=1+s/(2g_X−2).

sources.match: Lemma 28 compares the cusped volume vol′ and the compact volume vol on a curve in X(p)×X(p), using that both are sums of pullbacks from the two factors and that vol′−vol is a positive measure. The node defines the cusped measure coordinatewise, so that the comparison makes sense for curves meeting the cusps.

nodes.statement: For every effective curve cycle C⊂X(p)^r and measurable A on its normalization, 0≤vol′(C∩A)−vol(C∩A)≤C₀p⁻¹ vol(C). The total positive difference is O(p⁻¹) times compact volume. Its mass on any measurable subset is bounded by its total mass.

nodes.title: Hecke tubes away from cusps
nodes.statement: Prime-to-p Hecke branches are local isometries for h_Y. Outside compact cusp balls of radius (1/2−Aδ)ρ_X, compact and cusped metrics have a uniform comparison sufficient to carry an O(δρ_X) compact Hecke tube to an O(δρ_X) cusped tube. Apply the Hecke pull-push and then replace cusped by compact volumes with the uniform O(p⁻¹) error. The resulting ordinary diagonal tube estimate requires that the projected curve have no Hecke component, so its pull-push has no diagonal component. For a conjugate Hecke tube use the same holomorphic pull-push followed by the imported relative conjugate-diagonal bound. It needs no false divisor intersection with the real analytic locus; the large-radius sinh denominator gives the same p^(−1) gain.
proofSteps: Uniformize a branch of the isogeny correspondence by a positive real Möbius transformation; it is an isometry of the cusped metric.
Use the compact comparison and cusp-ball enlargement to ensure that each compared path stays in the allowed complement. Enlarge the constant A before fixing δ.

Apply the finite correspondence integration formula and the relative-diagonal estimate to the weighted pull-push. Check the no-diagonal-component condition by tracing it back to the original Hecke locus.
acceptance: Hecke maps are not asserted to be isometries of h_X.
A projected Hecke component fails the no-diagonal-component hypothesis and cannot be fed into this estimate.

sources.match: In the proof of Proposition 27 the authors use that T_k is étale on Y(p) and preserves h_Y, that h_X and h_Y agree up to a constant depending on δ outside (1/2−O(δ))ρ_X(p)-balls about the cusps, and so pass from a compact tube about τ_{g,k} to a cusped tube about T_k and, by pull-push, to the diagonal. The node states that comparison for both signs.

nodes.title: Big-diagonal multiplicity in the required non-Hecke setting
nodes.statement: There exist η>0,C,p₀ such that for every prime p>p₀ and effective curve cycle C⊂S², if C has no component in any Δ_g and both projected cycles pr_i*C are nonconstant and have no Hecke component, then Σ_g mult_{Δ_g}(C)≤Cp^{−η}Deg(C). For the gonality pullback both projected cycles are nonconstant and non-Hecke. The unrestricted statement for every curve outside the big diagonals is not used and is false on T₁×T₁.
proofSteps: Apply the imported double-diagonal point-volume estimate at radius δρ_X/2 and integrate the overlap dichotomy. The ordinary region contributes O(log p·p^{−δ})Deg(C).

For the ordinary and conjugate small-Hecke regions apply the signed Hecke-tube comparison to weighted projected cycles. Use cosh and sinh normalization respectively. Only the ordinary case needs the projected non-Hecke hypothesis; both give p^(−1) with p^(Aδ) losses.

For the bicusp region use the corrected rotation shell bound, signed three-bicusp repulsion, cusp-ball enlargement and the cusp count. The relative point-ball comparison is a separate HV.4 request: V(r)≤C_n(1+r)exp(r−R)V(R) for 1≤r≤R−2 and R<ρ_X. Its Green-identity proof is in the reader; absorb its O(log p) factor by a smaller fixed positive decay exponent. Split the area form into its two surface projections before estimating cusp overlap. For each projection and each original-radius bicusp centre, the other projected centres number p^(O(δ)); a fixed pair gives one order-p stabilizer coset, bounded by the rotation estimate. Apply the point-ball comparison to the weighted projected curve. The sum of enlarged projected ball volumes is bounded by 2vol plus p^(−1+O(Bδ))vol: when at least three projected centres occur, strengthened signed reconstruction places the point in one thin signed Hecke tube on the cusp complement. The cusp count and cosh/sinh tube comparison give the bound. The strengthened reconstruction conclusion includes both proximity to the signed locus and separation from all cusps. Choose the enlargement constant B to dominate original-radius losses, then δ so small that O(Bδ)<1/2. This avoids an unjustified product-ball overlap inference from three-bicusp repulsion. All polynomial logarithmic factors are absorbed by a smaller decay exponent. The reader gives the inequalities and their order of choices.

Before p grows choose δ>0 small enough for every previous lemma and Aδ<1/4. The sum of log p·p^{−δ}, p^{Aδ−1}, p^{−δ/2} and p^{Aδ−1/2} is O(p^{−η}) for η<min(δ/4,1/4). The reader records a counterexample to the published unrestricted formulation.

nodes.title: Symmetric powers of the quotient surface
nodes.statement: For n≥1 construct SymⁿZ(p)=Z(p)^n/S_n as a projective finite quotient, with its geometric-point cycle interpretation and characteristic-zero base-change compatibility. This uses a surface finite quotient, not the curve symmetric powers of JacobianChallenge. At the point-set level it agrees with Mathlib Sym; its scheme structure and the cycle morphism are supplied by the finite-quotient contract.
proofSteps: Take the permutation action on the n-fold product and descend the norm of an ample bundle. Apply the requested SF.1 finite quotient with an invariant projective embedding.

Identify orbits with effective degree-n zero-cycles. On finite flat degree-n families, construct the cycle map through local invariant functions/norms and glue; this is the precise relative cycle interface requested from SF.1.
Check characteristic-zero base change, product permutations and both determinant components; complex conjugation commutes with the algebraic quotient.
acceptance: Sym²Z is singular along the image of the diagonal of Z×Z, where the transposition fixes a codimension-two locus; it is still normal and projective.
Over a cycle [z₁]+…+[z_n] with distinct points the fibre of Zⁿ→SymⁿZ has n! points; over n[z] it has one.

nodes.title: Reduction to the normalization of the image
nodes.statement: A nonconstant map from a smooth connected curve B of gonality n to projective Z extends from its smooth completion and factors through the smooth projective normalization D of its integral image. One has gon(D)≤n, so it suffices to prove rigidity for a map birational onto its image. This includes nonproper B and maps of generic degree greater than one.
proofSteps: Use properness to extend across the finitely many omitted points, and the normalization universal property to factor through D.

For the generic finite map B̄→D push a degree-n pencil divisor to D. Its fibres are linearly equivalent by the norm of ratios of pencil functions. They vary, since a fixed finite support cannot contain the images of every fibre of a surjective finite map. The varying degree-n linear system contains a pencil, which after removing base points has degree ≤n.
This norm-pushforward gonality lemma belongs to HV.6 and is requested there; this node is its application to the quotient image.

nodes.title: The gonality-pencil cycle map
nodes.statement: Let B be smooth projective connected, f:B→Z birational onto its image, and h:B→P¹ a finite degree-n gonality pencil, n≥1. The fibre cycles f_*h⁻¹(t), with scheme multiplicities, define φ:P¹→SymⁿZ. It is nonconstant and generically degree one onto its image.
proofSteps: Apply the relative cycle map to the finite flat h and the graph of f. Finite maps of smooth curves are flat; ramified fibres carry their full local multiplicity.

On a dense open where f is injective and h is étale, two distinct fibres have disjoint images, so their cycles cannot coincide. Thus φ is generically injective, and in characteristic zero it is birational onto its image.
A change of basis in the pencil postcomposes h by PGL₂ and precomposes φ by its inverse, leaving the pulled-back covering construction isomorphic.
acceptance: For a hyperelliptic B with its double cover h, φ(t) is the sum of the images of the two points over t, and over each of the 2g+2 branch points φ(t)=2[f(b)].

sources.match: The proof of Theorem 29 takes the degree-n linear system on B to obtain φ:P¹→SymⁿZ(p), of degree one onto its image. The node constructs φ from the fibre cycles and proves those two properties.

nodes.title: A normalized pullback and its wreath stabilizer
nodes.statement: Let W=G^n⋊S_n act on S^n and let q:S^n→SymⁿZ be its finite quotient. For φ as above normalize an irreducible component of P¹×_{SymⁿZ}S^n dominating P¹, obtaining a smooth projective connected curve C with ψ:C→S^n and finite α:C→P¹. If H≤W stabilizes the chosen component, the induced action on its normalization has C/H≅P¹. Remove its action kernel when discussing effective local inertia. The component and H are choices; degree-weighted conclusions are independent of them.
proofSteps: Use finite base change, existence and finiteness of curve normalization. The map ψ is generically birational to its image because φ is birational onto its image.

Over the generic unramified locus, the finite quotient fibre is a single W-orbit and W permutes its irreducible components transitively. The stabilizer H acts transitively on the generic fibre in the chosen component, so its invariant function field is k(P¹).
Normalize the quotient and identify it with P¹ by the smooth proper curve/function-field dictionary. Do not assume an unramified pullback at branch points.
acceptance: Over the points of P¹ whose image avoids the branch locus of q the pullback is étale, so α:C→P¹ ramifies only over the finitely many remaining points.
For n=1, H is the stabilizer in PGL₂(F_p) of a component of the preimage of the rational curve in X(p)×X(p).

nodes.title: Weighted projection cycles and nondegeneracy
nodes.statement: Assume the image of B is not Hecke. Define C_i=(pr_iψ)_*[C] and C_ij=(pr_ijψ)_*[C] as weighted effective one-cycles, with multiplicity equal to generic map degree times image multiplicity. Every C_i is nonconstant and has no Hecke component, and every C_ij is contained in no Δ_g. One has Deg(C)=Σ_i Deg(C_i) and Σ_{i<j}Deg(C_ij)=(n−1)Deg(C). These facts hold for the actual chosen component and its stabilizer.
proofSteps: Connectedness of B and the monodromy of its degree-n pencil make the component stabilizer transitive on the n slots. Each slot maps dominantly to B’s image in Z, so cannot be constant or Hecke if that image is non-Hecke.
If C_ij lay in Δ_g then the corresponding quotient points in the generic fibre cycle would coincide. Generic h-fibres contain n distinct points and f is generically injective, excluding this.

Apply the canonical-degree projection formula. Each slot occurs once in the first sum and n−1 times among unordered pairs. All multiplicity bounds use these pushforward cycles rather than reduced images.
acceptance: For n=1 the pair sum is zero.
For n=2 its sole pair cycle has Deg(C_12)=Deg(C).
Check the non-Hecke hypothesis for both slots before applying the big-diagonal estimate.

sources.match: The proof of Theorem 29 sets C_i=π_{i*}C and C_ij=π_{ij*}C with multiplicities counting the degree of C over its image, and applies Propositions 25–27 to them. The node proves the nondegeneracy facts those applications need, including the non-Hecke projections required by the corrected Proposition 27 (finding E17).

nodes.title: Exhaustive wreath ramification support
nodes.statement: In the normalized pullback, every ramification point of α lies over either a CM⁺, CM⁻ or SBC point in some slot, or Δ_g^{ij} in two distinct slots for some g∈G. Here Δ_g^{ij} means simultaneous equality of both matched X coordinates. The list exhausts the finite wreath quotient inertia.
proofSteps: A nonidentity stabilizer element with trivial permutation has a nonidentity G element in a slot, so the quotient branch-locus theorem gives a special point there.

If the permutation is nontrivial, one of its moved slots is matched to another through a G transformation, producing Δ_g^{ij}. A point with free ambient W action has étale quotient neighborhood and cannot acquire ramification merely by pullback and normalization.
If the ambient stabilizer acts on several normalization branches, pass to the branch stabilizer; its effective action on the smooth curve gives the local ramification group.
acceptance: For n=1 the list reduces to CM⁺, CM⁻ and SBC; for n=2 the transposition composed with (g,g⁻¹) fixes ξ exactly when (x₁,y₁)=g(x₂,y₂), that is ξ∈Δ_g^{12}.

sources.match: The proof of Theorem 29 states that a point of C ramifies over P¹ only if its image lies on some Δ_g^{ij} or one of its projections is a singular bicusp or a CM point. The node is that exhaustive list.

nodes.title: Cyclic local indices with only one p factor
nodes.statement: For fixed n and prime p>max(5,n), effective local inertia of α is cyclic and has order ≤6n!p. If no slot is an SBC point its order is ≤6n!. The bound is linear in p, rather than p^n, even when several slots are bicusps.
proofSteps: An effective finite automorphism group of a smooth complex curve fixing a point acts faithfully on its tangent line, so local inertia is cyclic.

For an element of H, its n!th power has trivial permutation. Each remaining coordinate lies in a cyclic stabilizer of order dividing 2,3 or p. Their least common multiple divides 6p; without SBC it divides 6.
The order of the element therefore divides 6pn! or 6n!, respectively. Normalization only replaces ambient inertia by a subgroup/quotient and does not enlarge this exponent.
acceptance: Two order-p slot stabilizers contribute lcm(p,p)=p to a cyclic group, not p².

sources.match: The proof of Theorem 29 notes that the local stabilizer of a point of C is a cyclic subgroup of H, so the ramification index is O(p), and is at most 6n! when no projection is a singular bicusp. The node is that bound.

nodes.title: Ramification is negligible against canonical degree
nodes.statement: For fixed n and non-Hecke B as above, there are η_n>0,C_n,p_n such that Ram(α)≤C_np^{−η_n}Deg(C) for p>p_n. More precisely Ram(α)≪_n pΣ_i mult_SBC(C_i)+Σ_i(mult_CM⁺(C_i)+mult_CM⁻(C_i))+Σ_{i<j,g}mult_{Δ_g}(C_ij).
proofSteps: Use exhaustive support and the local-index bound, charging each ramified point at most a fixed n-dependent number of times. Each fibre cardinality is bounded by the corresponding branch multiplicity of the weighted projection cycle.
Apply the two CM estimates, the stronger p-weighted bicusp estimate and the corrected big-diagonal estimate; the nondegeneracy theorem supplies all projected non-Hecke hypotheses.
Use the degree sums and take the minimum of the finitely many positive exponents. Constants depend on n but not the particular curve or its map degree.
acceptance: Replacing p mult_SBC=o(Deg) by mult_SBC=o(Deg) fails to absorb cusp inertia.

sources.match: The proof of Theorem 29 bounds Ram(α) by p times the SBC multiplicities plus the CM and big-diagonal multiplicities of the projection cycles, and makes each term o(Deg C) by Propositions 26, 25 and 27. The node is that estimate with an explicit decay exponent.

nodes.title: The two Hurwitz inequalities contradict each other
nodes.statement: With D=Deg(C)>0, Riemann–Hurwitz for α is the exact equality 2g(C)−2=−2deg α+Ram(α)≤C_np^{−η_n}D. If d is the largest degree of the 2n coordinate maps C→X(p), then D≤2nd(2g_X−2), while Riemann–Hurwitz for that nonconstant projection gives 2g(C)−2≥d(2g_X−2)≥D/(2n). Choosing p so C_np^{−η_n}<1/(2n) is impossible.
proofSteps: The canonical-degree adapter gives the sum of the 2n projection degrees. At least one is positive, and g_X≥2 for p>5.
Apply the imported Riemann–Hurwitz theorem to α and independently to the largest nonconstant projection. Retain the negative −2deg α term in the equality and discard it only in the upper inequality.
Choose a single threshold dominating every previously fixed exponent and constant; divide by D>0. The lower and upper bounds are incompatible.
acceptance: For a degree-q unramified map to P¹ the formula gives 2g−2=−2q, not zero.
No factor 4π appears in the algebraic degree comparison D≤2nd(2g_X−2).

sources.locator: Proof of Theorem 29, last paragraph, p. 742
sources.match: The last paragraph applies Riemann–Hurwitz to α to get 2g(C)−2=o(Deg C) and to the projection of largest degree d to get 2g(C)−2≥d(2g_X−2)≫Deg(C), a contradiction. The node keeps the −2deg α term and writes the degree comparison without the factor 4π.

nodes.title: Bounded-gonality rigidity over C
nodes.statement: For every positive integer N there is M_N^geom such that for every prime p>M_N^geom, every smooth connected complex curve B with gon(B)<N and every nonconstant morphism B→Z(p) factors through an irreducible component of H_m for some m≥1 prime to p. Gonality means that of the smooth proper model. The statement covers both determinant components.
proofSteps: Reduce to the normalization of the image, with gonality still <N. If the image were non-Hecke, choose its degree-n pencil and the normalized pullback.
Apply the Hurwitz contradiction for each 1≤n<N and take the maximum of the finitely many thresholds. For N≤1 no positive gonality occurs, so the statement is vacuous.
Transport between the component presentations by the full projective group and the determinant-square-class comparison.
acceptance: For N=1 no curve has gonality <1 and the statement is vacuous.
The normalization of a component of H_m maps nonconstantly to Z(p) with Hecke image, consistent with the conclusion; the theorem says nothing about constant maps.

sources.locator: Theorem 3, p. 710; Theorem 29, p. 740, proof pp. 741–742
sources.match: Theorem 3 and Theorem 29 state that for p>M_N every nonconstant map from a smooth curve of gonality <N to Z(p) factors through a Hecke curve. The node is Theorem 29, for both determinant components.

nodes.title: Abramovich’s 7/800 bound from the imported numerical inputs
nodes.statement: For every congruence subgroup Γ≤PSL₂(Z) of finite index D, the compactified complex modular curve satisfies gon(X_Γ)≥7D/800. Interpret λ′₁=min(λ₁,1/4) by the supplied Friedrichs/continuous-spectrum convention, including no discrete eigenvalue below 1/4.
proofSteps: Import CongruenceSpectralGap:CSG.5/congruence-bound to obtain λ′₁≥21/100 for the effective congruence quotient.
Import Li–Yau in the finite-area singular-metric setting: λ′₁ Area≤8π gon. Import the Fuchsian area Area=πD/3.
Divide by 8π to obtain gon≥(21/100)D/24=7D/800. This application supplies the number; the general analytic and spectral results remain in their owners.
acceptance: Check (21/100)/24=7/800 exactly.
Do not apply the compact smooth metric spectral gap to the wrong quotient metric.

sources.match: Theorem 0.1 states gon(X_Γ)≥(7/800)[PSL₂(Z):Γ] for every congruence subgroup Γ; §§1.4–1.7 derive it from λ′₁≥21/100 (Luo–Rudnick–Sarnak), the Li–Yau inequality λ′₁A≤2A_c≤8π·gon for the singular hyperbolic metric, and A(X_Γ)=πD_Γ/3. The node is Theorem 0.1 assembled from the imported inputs.

nodes.title: Proper subgroup indices grow at least like p
nodes.statement: For prime p≥5 and every proper subgroup H<SL₂(F_p), [SL₂(F_p):H]≥p. The same conclusion holds for proper subgroups of PSL₂(F_p). In particular the minimum proper-subgroup index tends to infinity.
proofSteps: If the coset index d were <p, the action SL₂(F_p)→S_d kills every elementary transvection, because it has order p and S_d has no element of order p.
The pinned Tau Ceti transvection-generation theorem then makes the coset action trivial. A transitive trivial coset action has one coset, contradicting properness.
For PSL pull back a proper subgroup along the surjection from SL; its index is unchanged. This proof avoids a classification of finite simple groups or of maximal subgroups.
acceptance: A Borel has index p+1, consistent with the bound.
The proof requires p>d; divisibility by p in d! is the exact obstruction.

sources.locator: Remark after Theorem 2 and footnote 3, p. 710

A lower bound for the indices of proper subgroups is the group-theoretic input of that remark; the source gives no proof, and the node's elementary argument is this roadmap's.

nodes.title: Full SL₂ torsion monodromy on a bounded-gonality base
nodes.statement: For each N>0, every nonisotrivial elliptic scheme E/U over C with gon(U)<N has actual p-torsion image SL₂(F_p) whenever p>max(5,800N/7). The determinant is exactly one after choosing a Weil-pairing basis, because all pth roots of unity are constant. Changing the basis conjugates the image and does not change this conclusion.
proofSteps: Let H be the actual image. The level-frame torsor and moduli interpretation give a nonconstant classifying map U→Y_H, extending to the smooth proper modular quotient X_H. Its gonality is at most gon(U) by the generic finite-map gonality lemma.
The effective image H̄≤PSL₂ gives a congruence quotient of index D. If H̄ is proper, D≥p and the 7/800 bound contradicts gon(U)<N.

If H̄ is full but H is proper, the index of H in SL is at most two, contradicting the proper-index bound for p>3. Thus H is full. Do not replace actual image by projective or semisimplified image at the conclusion.
acceptance: The constant-j case is excluded because its moduli map need not be nonconstant.
An index-two lift of full projective image is explicitly ruled out.

sources.locator: Remark after Theorem 2 and footnote 3, p. 710; Abramovich Theorem 0.1, p. 1
sources.match: Page 710 and its footnote 3 state that the representations land in SL₂ because the Weil pairing is monodromy-invariant, and that for large p they are surjective onto SL₂(F_p) by the gonality bounds of Abramovich and Zograf. The node is that statement with the explicit threshold 800N/7.

nodes.title: An actual full-image representation has no quadratic self-twist
nodes.statement: Let p>3 and ρ:Π→SL₂(F_p) be surjective. If χ:Π→{±1} and an invertible linear A satisfy Aρ(γ)=χ(γ)ρ(γ)A for all γ, then χ is trivial. This is a statement about an actual intertwiner, not equality of projectivizations.
proofSteps: For γ in ker ρ the equation forces χ(γ)=1, since A is invertible and p is odd. Hence χ factors through SL₂(F_p).
Apply perfectness to the factored character. Scalar ambiguity in the choice of A is harmless; changing the basis conjugates the equation.
acceptance: Projectivizing the equation erases χ and cannot prove its triviality.

sources.match: Theorem 1 is phrased with an actual isomorphism of p-torsion local systems, not a projective or semisimplified one. The node is the group-theoretic fact that an actual intertwiner between a full-image representation and a quadratic twist of it forces the twist to be trivial; the source does not state it.

nodes.title: The classifying map from actual torsion data
nodes.statement: Let k be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, U/k a smooth connected curve, E,E′/U elliptic schemes and Ψ:E[p]≃E′[p] an isomorphism of finite étale F_p-module schemes. The triple gives a morphism f_Ψ:U→Z(p), with component determined by the Weil multiplier of Ψ modulo squares. Its projective class is used only to construct this map: the original Ψ remains part of the input. If E is nonisotrivial, f_Ψ is nonconstant. It extends uniquely from U to its smooth proper model because Z(p) is proper.
proofSteps: Étale-locally choose a full level basis of E[p], transport it through Ψ and take the diagonal quotient. Independence of the basis makes these local maps descend.
Projective rescaling of Ψ does not change f_Ψ, but may erase information needed for descent; retain Ψ separately. The first j-coordinate is the original j(E), so nonconstancy follows.
Use the valuative criterion of properness on the missing points of the smooth proper base. This is a map to the compact coarse surface, not an assertion of good reduction at those points.
acceptance: For E′=E and Ψ=[a] with a∈F_p^×, the map f_Ψ lands on H₁ for every a, since the projective class forgets scalars.
